title: Finally checked out Babylon (2022) - initial thoughts

commenti.body: I didn't quite love it, the setting felt very artifical it didn't feel like the 30s it felt like sets designed to look like the 30s. Guys like Tarintino and PTA kind of ruined all other historical because their films put such care into recreating the time period their set in. Chazelle didn't seem to know how to do that. Despite that I definitely enjoyed and I respected it a lot, at a time when it seems no new director wants to take any risks, he took a big swing, didn't quite hit a home run but a good enough. It annoyed me how harsh many critics were to it, with pretty much all of them saying it was to ambitious and because it didn't entirely match those ambitions it was a complete failure which I just think IS BS. Id rather watch someone failing to make a masterpiece, then someone making an average film well

Thing is... it's a sick, messy film. Not because Chazelle didn't meet its ambitions, but because BABYLON is a film born out of anxiety and fear—it's an anachronistic ride full of contradictions and confusions—because what it's depicting is confusing.

I'll always reference this 
[great review](https://www.frieze.com/article/damien-chazelle-babylon-2023) that I feel kind of describes what type of THING this movie is.

>"Hate it, for that's what the film demands. Love it too, for it also wants that. But not too blind a love. This object is still new, and we don't yet know what it contains."

""Beauty exists, but you won’t sense it here, says Babylon. It’s a misshapen, erratic, reviled, multi-faceted, overly earnest monstrosity, painfully and nervously self-aware of the gap between an emotion as experienced in real life and its fossil as captured by the Hollywood apparatus."

Don't really know how to describe it. I'm tired now, but you can check my long comment history full of discussions about this film.

I'll just say that this one deserves an outside-the-box kind of criticism (I'll make a post about this kind of criticism in few days probably).

>"Romance in Babylon, in the image of a depressed dance at a wedding between a Mexican self-destructive striver who simps an unattainable white woman, becomes another image to be glumly fed to the altar of Hollywood success."

THIS imperfection, is what makes BABYLON.

The opening party definitely felt too “extras hitting their marks.” Just found it off putting and it’s never a good feeling starting a film in the hole. It climbs out but that too self-conscious, artificial, over choreographed feel persists. I think Margot Robbie really carried the film. Felt like a pale imitation of The Day of the Locust.

There are beautiful moments. Jean Smart’s monologue, Margo Robbie crying on command. But the big spoiler is that if you have a basic knowledge of the transition from silents to talkies, you already know what’s going to happen. It’s an elephant in the room and parts feel like a based on a true story documentary which kills the thrill of the story. The worst part is that out of nowhere Tobey McGuire thing. I get that the theme is excess, but it adds so little to the main story. Babylon lacks focus in story so much that the predictable story just… doesn’t matter.
yes absolutely. To me, Babylon feels like someone recounting the story of Hollywood in that era to me, everything is a tad anachronistic or artificial because i'm recounting it, not living it.

I think we sometimes get too caught up in story when films are meant to be viewed. Films are not books, neither are they documentaries or nonfiction that should accurately reflect history.

Not saying that story isn’t important but overall it’s not the most important thing to me. That said Babylon is a fucking glorious mess of a spectacle. 

Probably my best movie going experience since BR 2049 and it will stick with me forever as such.
